observation.visible_scene: A static wide shot of an arid desert plain under a low, heavy storm cloud deck. A flat horizon with a small mesa/hill on the left and scattered shrubs in the foreground stays fixed throughout, indicating the camera does not pan. A bright rain shaft / virga column hangs on the right side of the frame, and a dark finger of cloud (a lowering) protrudes downward from the central cloud base. The upper sky shows a shifting bright gap with small blue patches.
visible_changes: The storm clouds continuously churn and deform: the dark cloud base undulates, the bright gap in the upper sky changes shape and drifts from the left toward the center/top as the segment progresses, and the overall cloud texture rolls and reorganizes frame to frame.

The central dark lowering beneath the cloud base elongates downward and thickens over the early-to-mid frames, then persists as a hanging cloud mass that slowly shifts slightly rightward; it is already present at the first frame and does not appear or vanish within the excerpt.

The rain shaft on the right remains present throughout but its column edges and position relative to the horizon move gradually rightward and widen/contract, tracking the drifting cloud system rather than being a fixed object.
Foreground desert, shrubs, and the left horizon hill show no motion, confirming the visible movement belongs to the clouds and precipitation, not the camera.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the rain shaft actually reaches the ground or is virga is not confirmable from these frames.
The storm's development before t=0 and its dissipation or movement after the last frame is unknown.
The true wind direction and speed driving the cloud drift are not directly measurable.
uncertain_details: Exact drift direction of the cloud mass is ambiguous because the bright upper gap and the lowering do not translate monotonically; motion appears partly rotational/churning rather than pure left-to-right translation.
The apparent rightward shift of the rain shaft and lowering is slow and could partly reflect internal cloud deformation rather than bulk translation.
This is a timelapse, so frame-to-frame cloud changes are compressed and intermediate motion between samples is not observed.
